Fibres/Yarns

BCI reports progress in sustainable cotton

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:38
Instaread

New global impact report highlights improvements in cotton farming practices, environmental performance and farmer livelihoods.

8th October 2026

Knitting Industry
 |  Geneva, Switzerland

Knitted Outerwear

The Better Cotton Initiative (BCI) has published its first Global Impact Report in five years, revealing measurable improvements in the environmental performance and profitability of cotton farming, while highlighting the challenges that remain in achieving consistent progress across different production regions.

Released on World Cotton Day on 7 October, the 2026 Global Impact Report draws on nine years of field-level data from the world’s largest cotton sustainability programme, which now represents almost a quarter of global cotton production.

The findings demonstrate improvements in synthetic fertiliser and pesticide use, greenhouse gas emissions, irrigation water consumption and farmer incomes following adoption of the BCI Standard.

This report is an unprecedented and transformative exercise by BCI, as it creates a first step for future programme delivery and deepened impact, with evidence that supports better informed data-driven decisions and scalable actions

According to the report, 69% of participating farmers reduced synthetic nitrogen use per kilogram of cotton, while 65% reduced their use of synthetic pesticide active ingredients per hectare. More than half, 54%, lowered their carbon footprint, while 52% of fully irrigated farms reduced the amount of irrigation water applied per kilogram of cotton.

The report also identifies improvements in farmer livelihoods, with 59% of smallholder farmers increasing their net income from cotton production since joining the programme.

BCI says the findings provide important evidence of how more sustainable agricultural practices can deliver environmental and economic benefits at scale, although the results also underline the complexity of achieving consistent improvements across diverse farming systems.

Nick Weatherill, CEO of the Better Cotton Initiative, said data and evidence were fundamental to strengthening the organisation’s impact and building confidence in more sustainably produced cotton.

“Data and evidence represent the most important currency with which we operate and form the foundation for all aspects of our work – enabling us to strengthen our impact at field level and building the trust and confidence of the market and stakeholders in BCI cotton,” he said.

The report also highlights progress in women’s participation within the programme. Women now account for 17% of field facilitation and producer unit management roles globally, compared with 9% five years ago.

More recent findings from the 2024-25 cotton season indicate that improvements are continuing. Compared with the previous season, 61% of BCI farmers reduced synthetic nitrogen use per kilogram of cotton, 40% reduced synthetic pesticide active ingredient use per hectare and 43% reduced irrigation water applied per hectare. Almost half, 49%, also reduced their carbon footprint.

However, BCI acknowledges that progress remains uneven, particularly in crop protection. While substantial improvements have been recorded among smallholder farmers, comparable reductions in pesticide use have not been consistently identified across larger farming operations.

The report also includes individual examples of farmers adopting more sustainable practices. Among them is Samina Khaskheli, a 37-year-old smallholder farmer from Pakistan’s Sanghar district, who has reduced her production costs by 15.6% after three years of implementing regenerative agricultural practices.

Iain Gardiner, BCI’s Senior Director of Impact and Development, said the organisation was committed to rigorous impact reporting based on reliable field-level information.

Working with farming communities and partners, BCI collects more than 20 million data points annually, supporting increasingly detailed analysis of agricultural practices and their environmental and economic outcomes.

“This report is an unprecedented and transformative exercise by BCI, as it creates a first step for future programme delivery and deepened impact, with evidence that supports better informed data-driven decisions and scalable actions,” Gardiner said.

Published alongside the Global Impact Report, BCI’s 2026 Annual Report provides further details of the organisation’s activities during the 2024-25 season.

During this period, BCI supported 1.4 million cotton farmers, who collectively produced 6.1 million tonnes of BCI cotton, equivalent to 23.87% of global cotton production.

The organisation’s Growth and Innovation Fund invested €18.5 million in supporting cotton farmers, including €17.8 million directed towards smallholders. The programme also reached 1.5 million field workers.

Over the past 16 years, BCI has worked with farming communities, textile supply chains, brands, government bodies and civil society organisations to encourage more sustainable cotton production. During that period, it has channelled €200 million into cotton-growing communities.

For textile manufacturers, yarn producers and apparel brands, the latest findings provide further evidence of the potential benefits of sourcing cotton produced under recognised sustainability standards, while reinforcing the importance of transparent measurement and continued improvement throughout the cotton supply chain.

BCI says the latest report will provide a foundation for future programme development, helping the organisation and its partners identify where interventions are delivering measurable results and where additional support is required.
